answer:
**KNN stores examples and postpones most modeling work until a query arrives.** A query is compared with stored points, the closest K are selected, and their labels or values are aggregated. This is why it is called lazy learning. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/user_guide.html)

If there are N stored points with d features, a brute-force query computes roughly Nd coordinate comparisons. Selecting neighbors adds work, and storage is O(Nd). Basic fitting can be little more than validating and storing data, though building a search index can be substantial.

**Nonparametric does not mean parameter-free.** The representation grows with the dataset instead of being summarized by a fixed-size coefficient vector. K, the distance metric, feature scaling, weighting, and index settings are still important choices.

For a large embedding catalog, vectorized brute force may be efficient on accelerators; tree or approximate indexes offer different build, memory, and recall tradeoffs. Benchmark the complete query path, including preprocessing. Keeping every training point also creates update and data-management requirements that a small fixed model may avoid.

**Technical details and references.**

kNN is “lazy” because it largely stores training examples rather than fitting a compact global prediction function. Its effective complexity can grow with the dataset, making it nonparametric. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/user_guide.html)

Brute-force prediction computes $N$ distances in $d$ dimensions, about $O(Nd)$, plus selection/aggregation; storing data costs $O(Nd)$. “Training” may just validate/store data, though building an index can be substantial. Trees or approximate indexes change query/build tradeoffs. Nonparametric does not mean no hyperparameters: $K$, metric, scaling, weighting, and index settings still need validation.
